name: Cuauhxicalli
material: Carved stone (basalt)
powers: Receptacle of sacrificial offerings at the temple.
description: A cuauhxicalli (Nahuatl 'eagle gourd bowl', from cuauhtli 'eagle' and xicalli 'gourd vessel') is a stone bowl that held the hearts of sacrificial victims in Aztec Tenochtitlan, placed before temple platforms where priests raised the still-beating heart to the sun before casting it into the vessel. Carvers shaped many examples as crouching eagles or jaguars with the bowl hollowed from the back; a celebrated andesite eagle cuauhxicalli found in the Templo Mayor precinct in 1985 measures some 139 centimetres. Others carry a sun disk carved inside and the earth goddess Tlaltecuhtli on the base, leading scholars such as Karl Taube to read the vessel as the earth's blood-filled womb receiving the sacrifice that renews the sun. The relief-covered Stone of Tizoc is sometimes identified as such a vessel, while the term also covers the reclining chacmool form that catches offerings on its belly. Spanish chroniclers and the colonial codices confirm the vessels' place at the centre of Mexica public ceremony.
source: Spanish chroniclers and Aztec codices

name: Temalacatl
material: Carved stone (basalt)
powers: Center of the gladiatorial sacrifice ritual.
description: The temalacatl was a great round stone disk set flat in an Aztec plaza as the stage for gladiatorial sacrifice, a rite tied to the festival of Xipe Totec in which a captive was bound, usually by a rope through the central hole, and made to fight successive armed warriors while holding only a feathered club. Bernal Diaz del Castillo, who watched the combat in Tenochtitlan, recorded the ordeal in vivid detail, describing how the exhausted captive was finally cut down and his body carried away. The best-known survivor, the Stone of Tizoc, is a basalt disk carved with the conquests of the emperor Tizoc and was dug up in 1791 during work on Mexico City's cathedral plaza. Because its shallow central depression could have held offerings, archaeologists have long debated whether such stones were true temalacatl or cuauhxicalli heart-vessels; Richard Townsend even suggests the depression may have been cut in the 16th century. Either way, the disk shows how Mexica sacrifice and imperial tribute were fused into public spectacle.
source: Bernal Díaz del Castillo and the Stone of Tizoc

name: Teponaztli
material: Hollow carved log with two tongues
powers: Speaks the voice of the gods at temple ritual.
description: The teponaztli is a horizontal slit drum made from a hollowed log whose H-shaped cut in the top produces two different pitches, struck with rubber-tipped sticks (olmaitl) rather than played by hand. Alongside the upright huehuetl it formed the core percussion of Aztec ritual music, and early accounts say its deep, carrying tone could be heard across Tenochtitlan during festivals, dances and war ceremonies. Fray Bernardino de Sahagun's Florentine Codex describes the instrument in detail, and colonial codices show pairs of players beating it before temple courtyards. Surviving examples, often carved from hardwoods, show that makers tuned the two tongues carefully and decorated the drum with religious carving. Similar twin-tongued slit drums were used across Mesoamerica, and the instrument survives in modified form in modern Mexican folk ensembles, its once-sacred festival role now largely secular.
source: Florentine Codex (Sahagún) and early accounts

name: Veracruz Hacha
material: Carved andesite or basalt
powers: Emblem of the Mesoamerican ballgame and its rituals.
description: A hacha is a thin, wide stone carving shaped like an axe head but with a deliberately blunt edge, produced in huge numbers by the Classic Veracruz culture of the Gulf lowlands between about 300 and 900 CE. Hachas take the form of human heads, often in profile, and animal faces, carved in fine andesite or basalt with great realism, and the finest examples come from sites such as El Tajin and the Remojadas region. Scholars read them not as working tools but as ballgame emblems, displayed with the great stone yokes and palmas worn by players in the Mesoamerican ballgame; the head-shaped hachas are thought by some to commemorate the severed heads of sacrificed players. Their varied faces make them a key record of Classic Veracruz religious imagery, linking the ballgame to sun worship and sacrifice. Hundreds survive in museums, prized as one of the finest portrait traditions of ancient Mexico.
source: Archaeological corpus of Classic Veracruz carvings

name: Jade Funerary Mask of Pakal
material: Jade mosaic with shell and obsidian eyes
powers: Guarantees the ruler's rebirth among the gods.
description: The funerary mask of K'inich Janaab' Pakal, the great seventh-century ruler of Palenque, is a mosaic of more than 340 pieces of green jadeite fitted over his face in the stone sarcophagus of the Temple of the Inscriptions. Discovered in 1952 by the Mexican archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier, the mask has eyes of shell and mother-of-pearl with pupils of black obsidian and stands about 25 centimetres tall. Jade carried deep meaning for the Classic Maya: the green stone evoked water, maize, the world centre and the breath of life, and the portrait is interpreted as showing the dead king reborn with the attributes of the maize god. Pakal's burial outfit contained around a thousand jade ornaments in all, including necklaces, bracelets, rings and a headband, marking jade as the supreme royal material. The mask and its companions now rest in the National Museum of Anthropology in Mexico City, where they are regarded as masterpieces of Mesoamerican art.
source: Excavation of Palenque, Temple of the Inscriptions (1952)

name: K'awiil Scepter
material: Carved stone or wood figure
powers: Invests the ruler with the lightning-god's authority.
description: The K'awiil scepter, often called the manikin scepter, is a short staff topped by a small figure of the Maya lightning god K'awiil, a deity shown with a mirror set in his forehead, an elongated snout and a serpent leg. Classic Maya rulers carried it as proof of divine kingship, and royal portraits at Copan, Tikal, Piedras Negras and Palenque show it held at accession and in dance rituals, its snake leg trailing to the ground. The forehead mirror links the scepter to the lightning that K'awiil sent forth, and the god himself belonged to the Palenque Triad of patron deities. Stelae record how the scepter was handed to a new king as part of the regalia that made him a living link between his people and the gods. Carved in stone or wood, its surviving depictions let scholars trace how the symbol of royal lightning passed across the Maya world over centuries.
source: Classic Maya stelae and painted ceramics

name: Chac Mool
material: Carved stone
powers: Receives offerings to the gods at the temple.
description: A chac mool is a reclining stone figure with its head turned to one side, knees drawn up and a flat basin held on its stomach, set at the entrances of temples across Mesoamerica from Toltec Tula to Aztec Tenochtitlan and Maya Chichen Itza. The basin served as a receptacle for offerings, and in Aztec contexts the figure is especially linked to the rain god Tlaloc and to the hearts and blood of sacrifice. The name was coined in 1875 by the explorer Augustus Le Plongeon, who found one at Chichen Itza and dubbed it 'chac mool' from Maya terms, so it is a modern label for figures whose original name is unknown. Famous examples include the Temple of the Warriors chac mool and several recovered from the Templo Mayor of Mexico City. The form appears to have spread with the Toltec-influenced art of the Early Postclassic, and modern replicas have made the reclining figure one of the most familiar images of ancient Mexico.
source: Augustus Le Plongeon and later excavations at Tula and Tenochtitlan

name: Tzompantli
material: Carved stone rack with wooden poles
powers: Displays the skulls of the sacrificed to the sun.
description: The tzompantli, from Nahuatl for 'skull rack', was a structure of wooden poles threaded with the skulls of sacrificial victims, erected beside Aztec temple platforms where daylight could display them to the sun. Spanish chroniclers were astonished by the great rack beside the Templo Mayor; Andres de Tapia counted the skulls in the tens of thousands, and Bernal Diaz described towers of them stacked in the ceremonial precinct. Excavations at the Templo Mayor uncovered the Huey Tzompantli, a carved stone platform of skull rows with hundreds of drilled skulls still mounted on wooden posts. The practice was not unique to the Aztecs: Maya centres such as Chichen Itza raised similar racks decorated with carved skulls. Beyond the macabre display, tzompantli were part of the Mesoamerican belief that sacrifice fed the sun and the earth, making the racks a public record of cosmic debt.
source: Spanish chroniclers and the Templo Mayor excavation

name: Obsidian Smoking Mirror
material: Polished obsidian disk
powers: Reflects visions and the smoke of divination.
description: Aztec priests and rulers used disks of highly polished obsidian as divination mirrors, gazing into the glossy black face for visions of what was hidden or to come. The name is inseparable from Tezcatlipoca, the 'Smoking Mirror', whose emblem was just such an obsidian mirror (tezcatl); his power to see everything was said to come through it. Fray Bernardino de Sahagun's Florentine Codex records seers and sorcerers working with mirrors, and carved examples survive with drilled holes for suspension, worn as pectorals or set in wooden frames with resin. Such mirrors were not only for seeing: because polished obsidian gathers the sun's heat, it could also be used in fire-making ritual. The black glass itself was sacred, a product of volcanic earth that the Mexica prized for knives, the eyes of effigies and the dark windows of prophecy. The smoking mirror remains a symbol of Tezcatlipoca's all-seeing, unpredictable power.
source: Florentine Codex (Sahagún)

name: Aztec Death Whistle
material: Molded clay
powers: Cuts through battle with a terrifying shriek.
description: The Aztec death whistle, sometimes called ehecachichtli or skull whistle, is a small clay whistle about three to five centimetres long, modelled as a human skull, whose internal chambers produce a shrill, wind-like and unsettling tone. The most famous examples were excavated in the late 1990s at Tlatelolco, clasped in the hands of a sacrificed man buried before a temple of the wind god Ehecatl, and they have been linked to both Ehecatl and the death god Mictlantecuhtli. Scholars such as Arnd Adje Both argue the original instruments mimicked the howling winds that Aztec souls met in the underworld rather than a human scream; the terrifying shriek heard in popular recordings comes from larger modern replicas. Whether they were blown in battle to frighten enemies is sometimes said but remains unproven, since none have been found on battlefields or in warrior graves. The whistle's grim fame has nonetheless made it a museum and internet sensation, with replicas sold worldwide.
source: Templo Mayor excavations and museum collections

name: Metate
material: Carved volcanic stone
era: From the preclassic era to the present
powers: Transforms maize into masa for the sacred staple tortilla.
description: The metate is the slightly concave stone grinding slab at the heart of Mesoamerican cooking, used with a hand-held stone (mano) to grind nixtamalised maize into masa for tortillas, tamales and atole. Basalt and other volcanic stone were preferred, and the craft of shaping the slab, often on carved supports or a tripod base, goes back to the Preclassic era and continues in rural households today. The grinding of maize was never mere kitchen work: Mesoamerican myth held that the gods made people from maize dough, as the Popol Vuh recounts, so the metate transformed the sacred staple into human food. Codices show women kneeling at the metate, and elaborately carved examples from later periods suggest the tool could also carry prestige. Modern lava-stone metates are still sold in markets across Mexico and Guatemala, prized for the flavour they give tortillas.
source: Mesoamerican codices and archaeological finds

name: Jade Bead Necklace
material: Jadeite beads
powers: Worn by rulers to embody the green of life and water.
description: Classic Maya rulers and nobles wore necklaces and collars of drilled jadeite beads, the green stone valued above all others in the Maya world and linked with rain, water, maize, the world centre and the breath of life. Royal portraits on stelae show long bead necklaces draped over the chest, often layered with earflare assemblies and bracelets of the same material. The richest evidence comes from tombs: the burial of K'inich Janaab' Pakal at Palenque held hundreds of beads and jade plaques, and the burial of the Red Queen of Palenque was accompanied by masses of jade beadwork. Jadeite itself was traded over great distances from highland sources in the Motagua River valley of Guatemala and elsewhere, and craftsmen drilled and polished it into tubes, spheres and carved pendants. The jade bead collar was thus both wealth and talisman, binding its wearer to the fertile green forces that sustained Maya life.
source: Classic Maya tombs and royal portraits

name: Comal
material: Flat clay disk
era: From the classic era to the present
powers: Toasts tortillas and maize cakes over the hearth.
description: The comal is a flat, round clay griddle set on three hearth stones and used to toast tortillas, roast seeds and warm tamales across Mexico and Guatemala. The word comes from Nahuatl comalli, and clay comales appear in Mesoamerican archaeological sites from the Classic period onward, showing the griddle's deep roots in the region's cooking. Colonial accounts describe the round hearth as the fixed centre of the household kitchen, the comal standing always over the fire beside the metate where maize was ground. Potters still shape comales by hand, and the clay version is prized because it gives tortillas a particular toasted flavour, though metal comales have become common. In the mythology of everyday Mesoamerican life the comal completes the arc from maize harvest to tortilla, and it remains a standard tool of the Mexican and Central American kitchen.
source: Archaeological finds and colonial accounts

name: Huipil
material: Cotton woven on a backstrap loom
powers: Carries the sacred patterns of the wearer's town and lineage.
description: The huipil is the loose cotton blouse woven and embroidered by Maya women of highland Guatemala, each town preserving its own colours, patterns and motifs that encode lineage, landscape and the sacred order. It is made on the backstrap loom, a pre-Columbian technology in which the weaver controls the tension with her own body, and the knowledge of patterns passes from mother to daughter. Motifs such as mountains, quetzal birds, suns and ancestors link the garment to Maya cosmology, and Ix Chel, the goddess of the moon and of weaving, is said to have taught the craft. Spanish colonial authorities taxed the garment and at times tried to suppress it, yet it survived and became a powerful emblem of Maya identity. Today huipiles are worn daily and at festivals across the highlands, and their woven patterns are studied by anthropologists as a living textile code.
source: Colonial records and living Maya weaving tradition

name: Dreamcatcher
material: Wooden hoop with woven netting and feathers
era: Ojibwe tradition; widely copied since the 20th century
powers: Catches bad dreams in its web and lets good ones through.
description: The dreamcatcher is a small hoop of willow or other wood bound with a web of netting and hung above a cradle, believed in Ojibwe tradition to catch bad dreams in its mesh while good dreams slip through the central hole to the sleeper below. The web form is tied to stories of the spider grandmother, a protective figure of Anishinaabe tradition, and early twentieth-century ethnographic accounts record such charms made for infants. Since the 1960s the dreamcatcher has been adopted across North America as a pan-Indian emblem and mass-produced as a souvenir, a development many elders and scholars caution has drifted far from its original use. The central opening matters: a web tied shut is sometimes said to hold bad dreams, while an open web lets them drain away. Modern Ojibwe and other Indigenous artists continue to make dreamcatchers in the traditional spirit, restoring its function as a guardian of children's sleep.
source: Ojibwe oral tradition and early ethnographic accounts

name: Calumet (Peace Pipe)
material: Stone bowl and wood stem, sometimes catlinite
powers: Binds treaties, prayers and peace in a single sacred act.
description: The calumet, or chanunpa in Lakota, is the sacred pipe of Plains peoples, a stone bowl joined to a wooden stem, smoked in ceremonies of prayer, treaty and peace. In Lakota tradition the chanunpa was given to the people by White Buffalo Calf Woman, who taught its songs and the meaning of its smoke as a bridge between humans and the sacred. The word 'calumet' came from French traders by way of a Norman term for a reed pipe, reflecting how early Europeans witnessed its power to seal alliances. Catlinite, the red pipestone of southwestern Minnesota, was traded widely for the finest bowls. A pipe was a living sacred object: its keeper followed strict rules, and to smoke together bound the parties to truth, as the famous peace-pipe ceremonies with colonial powers recorded. The pipe remains central to Lakota ceremony and has become a lasting symbol of Indigenous diplomacy.
source: Lakota oral tradition and early French accounts

name: Wampum Belt
material: Quahog and whelk shell beads woven into belts
era: Eastern Woodlands tradition to the present
powers: Records treaties and laws in a living web of shell.
description: Wampum belts are woven from cylindrical shell beads, the purple from quahog clam shells and the white from whelks, strung and woven into belts that served Eastern Woodlands peoples, above all the Haudenosaunee, as records of treaties, laws and history. Because the patterns carried meaning that had to be read aloud, wampum worked as memory in material form: the Hiawatha belt records the joining of the Five Nations, and the Great Law of Peace was both encoded in and recited over the belts. Colonial governments and missionaries also used wampum for diplomacy, while European traders turned the shell beads into a currency that flooded the market and reshaped their value. Strings and belts were exchanged to confirm a treaty or a condolence, and a belt given and accepted bound both sides to the words spoken over it. Haudenosaunee nations still hold and read ancient belts, and new belts are woven for modern agreements.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and colonial records

name: Kachina Doll
material: Carved cottonwood root with paint and feathers
powers: Brings the blessing of the katsinam spirits to children.
description: Kachina dolls, or katsina tihu in Hopi, are small figures carved from cottonwood root and painted with the attributes of the katsinam, the spirit beings who visit Hopi villages from the winter solstice until July. Given to children, especially girls, by katsina dancers, they are teaching objects rather than idols: each doll helps a child learn the identity, dress and power of a particular spirit. More than three hundred katsinam are known, from the gentle and humorous to the fierce ogre katsinam who discipline children. Since the late 1800s Hopi carvers have developed the craft into an internationally collected art, moving from small flat tihu to fully carved figures, yet the ceremonial gift remains the core of the tradition. To the Hopi the katsinam are ancestors and forces of the natural world, and the doll carries their blessing into the home.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Medicine Bag
material: Animal-hide pouch
era: Indigenous North America to the present
powers: Holds the personal medicines given to its owner in a dream.
description: The medicine bag is a small hide pouch carried or kept privately by many Plains and Woodlands people, holding the herbs, feathers, stones, roots or small objects revealed to its owner in a vision or dream. Unlike the communal sacred bundles kept by whole clans or societies, such as the Lakota pipe bundle, the medicine bag is personal: its contents are chosen by the spirits for one individual and are usually kept secret. Its power, elders say, depends on how faithfully the owner follows the instructions that came with the vision, and careless handling is believed to drain or endanger that power. Ethnographic accounts record that the bag is never opened lightly, is not shown to others without reason, and is often buried with its owner or passed on with ceremony. The bundle tradition underlies much of the healing and 'medicine' concept that travellers, traders and missionaries encountered across the continent.
source: Plains and Woodlands oral tradition and ethnography

name: False Face Mask
material: Carved basswood with red and black paint
powers: Wards off sickness with the power of the forest spirits.
description: The False Face masks of the Haudenosaunee are distorted human faces carved from living basswood, painted red and black, and used by the False Face Society in curing ceremonies that drive sickness from the sick. The twisted features recall the forest beings of tradition, above all the Great Face who is said to have broken his own face in a contest with the sun and gained power over disease, appearing in the story of the Flying Head. Traditionally the masks are carved from the living tree without metal tools, so the bark and spirit of the tree remain part of the carving, and they are kept by society members where tobacco can be offered to them. Historically the masks were never sold; their acquisition by museums and collectors in the late twentieth century became a major controversy, and some collections have since returned them. Worn by dancers who blow warm ashes over the patient, the masks embody the being that both causes and cures sickness.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and ethnography

name: Yeibichai Mask
material: Painted buckskin with feathers and turquoise
powers: Lets a dancer embody a Holy Person in ceremony.
description: The yeibichai masks of the Navajo are painted buckskin masks worn by dancers in the Nightway, the great nine-night healing ceremony, so that the wearer may embody a Holy Person, or ye'i, such as Talking God (Yeibichai) or Water Sprinkler. Made anew for each ceremony under strict rules and handled only by initiated singers and dancers, the masks carry the facial markings, colours and headgear that identify each Holy Person to the community. The Nightway chants invoke the blessing of the Holy People and call on Changing Woman, the great female deity of Navajo tradition, and the other powers of the Fourth World. Because the masks are so sacred, they are traditionally never sold, displayed publicly or photographed, and knowledge of their making is closely guarded. In the ceremony the masked dancers' final public dance is itself called the Yeibichai, the vivid climax of a rite meant to restore balance and health.
source: Navajo oral tradition and ceremonial practice

name: Birchbark Canoe
material: Birchbark over cedar frame with spruce root lashing
powers: Glides silently over lakes and rivers, light enough to carry.
description: The birchbark canoe, wiigwaasi-jiimaan in Ojibwe, is the light, silent and remarkably strong craft built of sheets of birchbark sewn over a cedar frame with spruce root and sealed with spruce gum, the great carrier of the Anishinaabe and other northern peoples. Light enough for one person to carry across a portage, a full canoe could still move families, furs and goods across hundreds of miles of lakes and rivers, which is why French traders and the voyageurs adopted it wholesale. Master builders selected a smooth-barked birch, stripped the bark in the right season, and shaped the craft with the same materials and joinery used for centuries. The canoe also runs through the region's stories, from the flying canoe of the Passamaquoddy to the journeys of culture heroes. Today a handful of carvers still build bark canoes, and museums preserve the finest examples of this northern engineering triumph.
source: Anishinaabe oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Cedar Bark Basket
culture: Haida, Tlingit and other Northwest Coast peoples
material: Woven cedar bark and root
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Holds water itself when woven tight enough.
description: Northwest Coast weavers, above all Haida, Tlingit and Tsimshian women, weave baskets and hats from shredded cedar bark and split cedar root, some so tightly that they hold water and can be used for cooking by dropping hot stones into the liquid. The twined technique, in which wefts are twisted around warp strands, produces the fine diagonal patterns that distinguish each nation's basketry, from simple checkerwork to complex animal and mountain designs. Cedar itself is honoured as a giver: in Haida tradition the cedar tree appears as Ts'uu Jaas, the Cedar Woman, a supernatural being whose generosity gave people the bark, wood and root for their tools and homes. Weavers harvest the inner bark in spring with prayers and care, taking only what the tree can spare. The art continues, and master weavers' baskets are now sought after by museums and collectors.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and ethnographic collections

name: Totem Pole
material: Carved western red cedar
era: Northwest Coast tradition to the present
powers: Proclaims clan lineage and stories in carved cedar.
description: Totem poles are tall carvings made from whole trunks of western red cedar, raised by the Haida, Tlingit, Tsimshian, Kwakwaka'wakw and other Northwest Coast peoples before houses, at graves and as welcome or memorial figures. The carved animals and beings are not idols but crests: they record a clan's lineage, its founding ancestors and the supernatural helpers who saved them, and a pole is read by those who know the family's history. House poles stood against the front of a big house, mortuary poles held an ancestor's remains, and the figures often include raven, eagle, bear, wolf, whale and thunderbird. Canadian law banned the potlatch in 1884, and carving declined sharply, but the art was revived in the twentieth century and has become a proud symbol of Indigenous identity across the region. New poles are still raised today with ceremony and feasting, continuing an unbroken tradition of sculptural storytelling.
source: Northwest Coast oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Thunderbird Club
material: Carved wood
powers: Carries the strike of the thunderbird into battle.
description: The thunderbird club is a heavy carved club whose grip and head take the form of a great bird, most often the thunderbird, so that each blow falls with the power of the being whose wingbeats make thunder and whose flashing eyes cast lightning. Carried by chiefs and warriors of the Northwest Coast and some Plains nations, the club is both a weapon and an emblem, its carved beak, wings and tail binding the bearer to the great sky bird of the origin stories. Because the bird's image was itself charged with power, such a club was a personal and often hereditary treasure. The thunderbird appears across the continent in different guises, and its image on a weapon proclaimed that the bearer struck with the force of the storm. Surviving clubs are treasured in museum collections as masterworks of Native carving.
source: Northwest Coast and Plains oral tradition

name: Coup Stick
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Crow and others)
material: Long decorated staff or lance
powers: Touching the enemy is the highest act of bravery.
description: The coup stick, or counting-coup staff, is a decorated staff or lance carried by Plains warriors such as the Lakota, Cheyenne and Crow for the act of 'counting coup', touching an enemy in battle without killing him. Among the Plains peoples touching a living enemy was ranked the bravest feat of war, above killing, and each time a warrior counted coup he added an honour, often marked on the staff with an eagle feather. The four grades of war honour were carefully ranked, and a man could also count coup on enemies' horses or possessions. Such sticks were wrapped with cloth and fur, hung with feathers, and treated with the respect due a record of personal bravery. Ethnographers recorded how these honours were proclaimed at dances, and the staff became the physical tally of a warrior's reputation.
source: Plains oral tradition and ethnography

name: War Bonnet
culture: Plains peoples (Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfoot and others)
material: Eagle feathers on a hide cap or band
powers: Each feather marks an honor earned in war or ceremony.
description: The war bonnet, or eagle-feather headdress, is the grand plume of upright golden-eagle feathers worn by honoured leaders of the Plains nations such as the Lakota, Cheyenne, Blackfoot and Crow. Each feather had to be earned, given for an act of bravery, a coup counted in battle, or received through a vision, and the bonnet itself was assembled with ceremony. The straight-up bonnet with its long trailer familiar from photographs became prominent in the nineteenth century; earlier and regional forms varied widely, including buffalo-horn bonnets and feather roaches. Feathers could be awarded for peace and generosity as well as war, and the bonnet marks its wearer as a man or woman of proven standing, worn with the responsibility that leadership carries. The style has since been imitated widely in popular culture, but among Plains peoples the bonnet remains a serious, earned honour.
source: Plains oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Medicine Wheel
material: Arranged stones in a circle with spokes
era: From at least the late prehistoric era
powers: Mirrors the four directions and the circle of life.
description: The medicine wheel is a circle of stones laid out on high plains ground with lines of stones radiating from the centre like spokes, read by Plains peoples as a sacred map of the cosmos, the four directions, the seasons and the circle of life. The most celebrated example, the Bighorn Medicine Wheel in Wyoming, measures some 23 metres across and has 28 spokes, and studies have suggested its outer cairns may align with the summer solstice and stars, though the precise purpose of the old sites remains debated. Similar wheels at Moose Mountain in Saskatchewan and elsewhere show the form was widespread. Modern Plains nations still use stone circles as places of prayer and ceremony, and the wheel's four directions have become a teaching symbol for balance and guidance. Whatever its original astronomy, the medicine wheel endures as a model of harmony between people and the land.
source: Plains oral tradition and archaeological study

name: Katsina Owl Doll
material: Carved cottonwood root with paint
powers: Teaches children the ways of the night hunter spirit.
description: The owl katsina doll, or mongwau tihu in Hopi, is a carved and painted cottonwood figure of the owl spirit of the Hopi katsinam, given to children so they may learn the owl's identity and power. The owl is a night hunter whose eyes and voice mark it as a being of wisdom and, in some traditions, a messenger connected to the spirit world. Like all katsina tihu the doll is carved from the soft root of the cottonwood, a wood the Hopi link to water and moisture, and painted with the colours and markings of the particular spirit. The owl katsina appears among the hundreds of katsinam who visit the villages in season, and its doll carries the teaching of that visit into the home. Collectors prize such carvings, but to the Hopi the doll's first purpose remains the instruction of children in the ways of the spirits.
source: Hopi oral tradition and ethnographic studies

name: Three Sisters Garden
culture: Haudenosaunee and other Eastern Woodlands peoples
material: Interplanted corn, beans and squash in mounds
powers: The three crops support each other as the sisters did the people.
description: The Three Sisters garden is the Haudenosaunee method of planting corn, beans and squash together in a single mound, each crop supporting the others: the corn stalk gives the beans a pole to climb, the beans fix nitrogen in the soil for the corn, and the squash spreads its broad leaves to shade the roots and hold moisture. The three crops are called the sisters, or Deohako in Iroquoian tradition, inseparable companions given to the people by the Creator, and they are honoured in ceremonies through the growing season, especially at the Green Corn Festival. The system fed the Haudenosaunee confederacy for centuries and is today studied as a model of sustainable companion planting. Stories of the three sisters carry the moral of mutual support, and many modern gardeners and Indigenous food movements have revived the mounds. The garden remains the living foundation of Haudenosaunee agriculture and identity.
source: Haudenosaunee oral tradition and agricultural history

name: Inukshuk
material: Stacked stones
powers: Guides travelers and marks the good hunting ground.
description: The inuksuk, often spelled inukshuk, is a figure of stacked stones built by the Inuit and other Arctic peoples as a landmark in landscapes where trees offer no bearings; the Inuktitut name means 'something that acts in the capacity of a human'. Inuksuit marked travel routes, safe crossings, good hunting and fishing places, food caches and camps, and their shapes could carry messages, from the direction to point to a warning of danger. In northern Alaska the Inupiat built lines of them to herd caribou toward hunters. The human-shaped form is properly an inunnguaq, but the simpler inuksuk on the flag of Nunavut has made the stone figure an emblem of the Arctic and of Canada as a whole. Inuit still build them today, and the pattern appears on the Vancouver Olympics emblem, in art and in jewellery.
source: Inuit oral tradition and Arctic ethnographic records

name: Hex Sign
material: Painted wooden or tin barn disk
powers: Wards off harm and invites luck on the barn.
description: Hex signs are the painted circles and eight-point stars fixed to Pennsylvania Dutch barns from the 18th century onward, their bright patterns of tulips, hearts, distelfinks and stars drawn from the folk art and fraktur of German-speaking settlers. The word 'hex' comes from the German Hexe, 'witch', and many outsiders came to believe the signs were charms to ward off witchcraft, bad luck and fire; in local Pennsylvania German, 'hex' can also mean 'spell'. Scholars argue that the protective meanings were largely a popular invention layered over decoration, though some symbols such as stars clearly carried good-luck associations. Painted by barn artists on the large gable-end 'banks' of Swiss-German barns, the signs became a regional icon of southeastern Pennsylvania. Today hex signs are a celebrated folk art, reproduced on houses, businesses and souvenirs across Berks County.
source: Pennsylvania Dutch folk art and regional studies

name: Jack-o'-Lantern
material: Carved hollow pumpkin with a candle
era: Irish tradition; American form since the 19th century
powers: Keeps the wandering soul of Jack at bay with its light.
description: The jack-o'-lantern is a hollowed pumpkin carved with a face and lit from within, set out at Halloween as the American descendant of the Irish carved-turnip lantern of 'Stingy Jack'. In the legend Jack tricked the Devil and was barred from both heaven and hell, left to walk the dark with only a burning coal inside a hollowed turnip, and the bog-lights of swamps were long called jack-o'-lanterns after him. Irish and Scottish immigrants carried the tale to North America in the 19th century, where the larger, easier-to-carve native pumpkin replaced the turnip. The practice absorbed older Celtic traditions of lighting Samhain fires, and by the early 1900s pumpkin carving was a fixture of American Halloween. The jack-o'-lantern has since become a global symbol of the season, carved each October with faces ranging from folk-mask grins to elaborate art.
source: Irish-American Halloween folk tradition

name: Gris-Gris Bag
material: Red flannel pouch with herbs, roots, coins or stones
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Carries the working of the root doctor for love, luck or protection.
description: The gris-gris bag is a small flannel pouch, often red, filled with herbs, roots, coins, stones or personal items and made by Louisiana root doctors and hoodoo practitioners to carry a 'work' for love, luck, money, protection or success. The name gris-gris is used in New Orleans, while the same charm is known as a mojo bag or hand elsewhere, and the tradition blends West African spiritual practice with colonial folk belief. A bag must often be 'fed' with oils, powders or an offering to keep its power, and it is carried on the body, usually in a pocket or at the waist, and kept secret. Roots such as High John the Conqueror are among the classic ingredients, and the making of a bag follows precise instructions about days, colours and prayers. Gris-gris remains part of New Orleans culture and the Voodoo-hoodoo exchange, a portable connection to the conjure tradition.
source: Louisiana hoodoo tradition and ethnographic records

name: Haint Blue Paint
material: Pale blue-green paint, traditionally with indigo or lime
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Keeps haints, the wandering spirits, from entering the house.
description: Haint blue is the pale blue-green paint used on porch ceilings, doors and window frames of Gullah homes in the Lowcountry of South Carolina and Georgia, said to keep haints, the restless spirits of the dead, from entering the house. Water is traditionally the veil between the living and the dead, and the blue is read as the colour of water that haints cannot cross; the eerie 'boo hag' who slips in through keyholes is among the beings the colour is meant to repel. Some writers also trace the hue to practical roots, noting that the lime-based blue paint helped repel insects and resist damp, and that indigo dye was a staple of Lowcountry plantations. The custom has spread far beyond the Sea Islands into a popular Southern decorative style, with paint companies selling shades called haint blue. For the Gullah, the paint remains a visible sign of a protective, deeply held worldview.
source: Gullah oral tradition and regional studies

name: Witch Bottle
material: Stoneware or glass bottle with pins, nails, hair and urine
powers: Traps the witch's harm and turns it back on her.
description: The witch bottle is a stoneware or glass bottle packed with pins, needles, nails, broken glass, hair and often urine, sealed tightly and hidden in a wall, chimney, hearth or floor of a home to protect it from witchcraft. The practice, brought from England and Europe to colonial America, worked by drawing the witch's curse into the bottle and then returning the harm to its sender; the pins and sharp contents were meant to wound the witch who sent the spell. Scores of such bottles have been excavated from colonial American buildings and English houses, often dating from the 17th to the 19th centuries, and similar 'spirit bottles' were buried to trap demons and fairies. Folklore says the bottle should be kept in the dark and never opened or broken, or the trapped harm is released. The witch bottle is among the most archaeologically visible forms of folk magic in the Anglo-American world.
source: Colonial American folk magic and archaeological finds

name: Sweetgrass Basket
material: Coiled sweetgrass with palmetto fronds
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Carries the memory of African weaving in every coil.
description: The sweetgrass basket is the coiled basket of the Gullah people of the South Carolina Lowcountry, woven from sweetgrass with palmetto fronds and longleaf pine needles, a craft carried from West Africa to the American rice coast. The tight coil stitch descends directly from West African prototypes, and for centuries the baskets were practical tools, above all the broad fanners used to winnow rice on the coastal plantations. Weavers of Mount Pleasant and the Sea Islands passed the skill from generation to generation, and by the late 20th century the baskets were recognised internationally as fine art, collected by museums and buyers. Modern weavers still harvest sweetgrass by hand with respect for the plant, and the baskets remain a living emblem of African continuity in the Americas. The sale of the baskets along Highway 17 has made them a familiar sight and a powerful symbol of Gullah heritage.
source: Gullah weaving tradition and cultural studies

name: Kero
material: Carved wood, often with painted scenes
powers: Twin cups shared to seal alliance and honor the sun.
description: The kero is the paired ceremonial drinking cup of the Andes, a flared goblet most often carved from wood, drunk from in twos at rituals of alliance, hospitality and the great festivals of the Inca calendar. The paired cups were passed so that each party drank the other's offering, sealing friendship and reciprocal obligation, and the drink was usually chicha, the maize beer central to Andean ceremony. Inca nobles and officials received keros as marks of office, and the cups appear in colonial accounts as indispensable to the toasts that accompanied every treaty and celebration. After the Spanish conquest, colonial-era keros were painted with elaborate scenes of Inca life, rulers, animals and ceremony, creating a crucial record of how the empire remembered itself. The kero tradition survives among Andean communities, where the paired cup still seals the bonds of ayllu and fiesta.
source: Inca-period and colonial keros in museum collections

name: Tumi
material: Gold, silver, copper or bronze
powers: Sacrificial blade of the priests under the moon.
description: The tumi is the crescent-bladed ceremonial knife of the Andes, a wide arched blade of gold, silver, copper or bronze on a rectangular handle, used for sacrifices and depicted in Moche art cutting the throat of victims. Later Sican and Lambayeque metalworkers made ornate gold tumis crowned with the figure of Naylamp, the mythic founder of the Lambayeque dynasty shown as a bird-man, and the knife passed into Chimu and Inca ritual. The most famous example, the Tumi of Illimo or of Lambayeque, is a gold blade about 41 centimetres tall weighing nearly a kilogram, recovered from Huaca Las Ventanas at Batan Grande in 1936. Because most known examples are of precious metal, scholars believe they were largely symbolic, displayed in ritual and buried with lords rather than used for daily work. In modern Peru the tumi has become the national symbol of the country, reproduced in folk art, tourism souvenirs and even the emblem of the Peruvian College of Physicians.
source: Lambayeque/Sicán and Inca archaeological finds, including the Tumi of Lambayeque (1936)

name: Quipu
material: Colored and knotted cotton or camelid cords
era: Andean tradition to the colonial era
powers: Records numbers, tribute and histories in knots.
description: The quipu, or khipu, is the knotted-cord record-keeping system of the Andes, in which a main cord holds pendant cords whose colours, knot positions and spacings encode information, read by trained officials known as khipu-kamayuq. The Inca empire used quipus to keep accounts of tribute, census, harvests, armies, calendars and storerooms, and Spanish chroniclers called them the 'books' of the empire, records the colonial government could not match. Scholars have shown that the knots encode numbers in a decimal positional system, and a growing minority argues some quipus also carried narrative and genealogical meaning, though that reading remains debated. The cords were made of cotton or camelid fibre, and hundreds of examples survive, many unearthed from coastal tombs and highland caches. The Spanish destroyed thousands of quipus, yet some Andean communities continued to use them into the twentieth century, and the khipu has become a powerful symbol of Inca civilisation and of a knowledge system nearly lost.
source: Colonial chronicles and surviving Inca quipus
